panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 5 panels (A, B, C, D, E). A: Coronal T2WI in 12-year-old with PHACE syndrome showing posterior fossa malformation explicitly described in caption. B: MRA panel showing cerebral arteriopathy - carotid thinning and rete mirabile - in PHACE syndrome case. C: MRA lateral view showing same PHACE arteriopathy with carotid thinning and tortuous irregular vessels. D: Axial MRA MIP showing PHACE cerebral arteriopathy with carotid thinning and rete mirabile. E: Skull-base CT showing narrowed right internal carotid canal signaling carotid hypoplasia, a manifestation of PHACE cerebral arteriopathy.
panels.attribution_text: PIZZATTO et al. Arteriopathy in pediatric stroke: an underestimated clinical entity.. Arquivos de neuro-psiquiatria 2021. doi:10.1590/0004-282x-anp-2020-0105. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 9.
panels.figure_caption: PHACE syndrome in 12-year-old female with a right-face hemangioma. Coronal T2WI (A) shows asymmetry of cerebellar hemispheres with volumetric reduction of the right hemisphere and hypoplastic vermis. MRA (B, C and D) shows thinning of the right internal carotid artery and multiple tortuous and irregular ipsilateral vessels (rete mirabile). CT of the skull base (E) depicts narrowing of the right internal carotid canal (arrow), thus signaling hypoplasia.
in_text_mentions: PHACE syndrome comprises a spectrum of anomalies, including posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, eye anomalies and sternal cleft or supraumbilical raphe (Figure 9). For a definitive diagnosis of PHACE syndrome, the patient needs to present a infantile hemangioma on the face or scalp > 5 cm51.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: MRA panel from a PHACE syndrome case series showing tortuous right internal carotid and posterior cerebral arteries, i.e., an intracranial/cerebrovascular arterial anomaly (the C component of PHACE); arrows 1 and 2 annotate the tortuous vessels. Disease attribution is supported by the PHACE-focused article title and the caption's explicit MRA description. B: Clinical photograph of case 3 showing sternal aplasia and thoracic cutis aplasia, corresponding to the sternal defect (S) component of PHACE syndrome; the caption explicitly ties the image to a PHACE syndrome case. Skin tone judged from the visible, adequately lit chest skin.

in_text_mentions: Physical examination revealed a prominent capillary hemangioma of the left eyelid and milder right-sided involvement, as well as a supraumbilical raphe (Figures 2, 3). Initial labs noted an incidental urinary tract infection (UTI). After review of outside imaging, given concern for possible PHACE syndrome, the patient was admitted to the general pediatric inpatient team for further imaging studies and inpatient consultations by ophthalmology, dermatology, and genetics.

panels.body_site: face (left V1 trigeminal distribution, nasal bridge)
panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a neonate showing an extensive segmental facial hemangioma in the left V1 (ophthalmic) trigeminal distribution extending to the nasal bridge, a hallmark cutaneous feature of PHACE syndrome. The article is a systematic review and case report focused on PHACE syndrome, and the caption and in-text explicitly attribute this facial phenotype to the disease. The image is a real patient photograph with an anonymization bar over the eyes; the visible skin appears light. Segmental facial infantile hemangioma in a trigeminal distribution is a classic (textbook) presentation of PHACE syndrome.

panels.rationale: A clear clinical photograph of an infant with a large, untreated segmental plaque-morphology facial hemangioma on the right side of the face, explicitly described in the caption and in-text as the typical hemangioma finding in a case report of PHACE syndrome. The image is a real patient image, not a diagram or other-disease comparison, and the manifestation is directly attributable to the configured target disease.

panels.figure_caption: Picture of the Patient. Photography of the patient in infancy before treatment of the haemangioma. At this stage, PHACE syndrome could already have been suspected due to the typical finding of a segmental hemangioma.
in_text_mentions: The patient had a history of a congenital right-sided facial hemangioma of plaque-morphology (Figure 2). This was treated in infancy with interferone- followed by laser therapy. The clinical examination revealed a prepubertal stage (Tanner PH1, B1).

findings.label: Posterior fossa malformation on brain MRI
findings.evidence: Caption: 'Brain MRI with contrast showed left cerebellar hypoplasia and an enlarged infratentorial subdural space. Cerebellar hypoplasia may contribute to potential developmental delays, balance difficulties, and neurological deficits in PHACE syndrome.' In-text: 'left cerebellar hemisphere hypoplasia, enlargement of the left fourth ventricle lateral recess, and an increased infratentorial subdural space extending along the left cerebral hemisphere (Figure 2).'

panels.rationale: Single axial contrast brain MRI of a real patient showing left cerebellar hemisphere hypoplasia with an enlarged infratentorial subdural space, explicitly attributed by the caption and in-text to PHACE syndrome (posterior fossa malformation). The contrast-enhancing cerebellopontine cistern mass (acoustic neuroma/vestibular schwannoma) is described as Figure 3, not this panel, so this panel is tagged phace_syndrome only. No age or ethnicity stated in caption or in-text.

plate_findings.evidence: Dandy Walker Cyst Associated with Hypoplastic Vermis and Right Cerebellar Hemisphere

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: T1 MRI brain axial view in infant with PHACE syndrome per article title 'Large destructive facial hemangioma in PHACE syndrome' showing captioned Dandy-Walker cyst with hypoplastic vermis, matching posterior fossa malformation vocabulary. B: T1 MRI brain sagittal view in same infant with PHACE syndrome showing captioned Dandy-Walker cyst/posterior fossa anomaly, matching posterior fossa malformation vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Nagdeve and Mudkhedkar. Large destructive facial hemangioma in PHACE syndrome.. Journal of Indian Association of Pediatric Surgeons 2009. doi:10.4103/0971-9261.57704. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: (T1 Weighted Images of MRI Brain): Dandy Walker Cyst Associated with Hypoplastic Vermis and Right Cerebellar Hemisphere
in_text_mentions: Echocardiography showed osteum secundum type of atrial septal defect (ASD). Doppler studies of carotid and subclavian arteries were normal. Contrast Enhanced computed tomography (CECT) and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) of brain showed the presence of Dandy Walker cyst associated with hypoplastic vermis and right cerebellar hemisphere [Figure 2]. MR-angiography was normal. The baby was administered oral antibiotics and prednisolone 2mg/kg/day along with oral ranitidine.

panels.rationale: T2-weighted brain MRI in PHACE syndrome case showing cerebellar dysplasia on right side, which maps to posterior fossa malformation vocabulary term; large arachnoid cyst indicated by arrow is not in vocabulary so listed as proposed.
panels.attribution_text: Denzer et al. A case of phace syndrome and acquired hypopituitarism?. International journal of pediatric endocrinology 2012. doi:10.1186/1687-9856-2012-20. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Arachnoidal cysts. MRI Scan of the brain. Coronar, T2-weighted. Cerebellar dysplasia is seen on the right side. The arrow indicates a large arachnoidal cyst.
in_text_mentions: MRI of the brain confirmed the findings of complex structural cerebral- and cerebrovascular arterial anomalies with cerebellar dysplasia on the right side, deformation and dislocation of the brain stem, and aplasia of the right carotid (Figure 3). The empty sella (Figure 4) appeared to be caused by dorsal displacement of the infundibulum by arachnoidal cysts, which were stable in size over the course of one year. Cranial of the neurohypophysis a structure that appears to be a considerably reduced adenohypophysis was identified.
